This vignette walks through the disease- / condition-group comparison workflow in spatialCooccur. The pattern is:

  1. Collect per-sample spatial transcriptomics data (one image per sample, or multiple images grouped by patient).
  2. Compute a spatial co-occurrence score per sample with one of the *_per_sample() helpers.
  3. Test for differences between groups (e.g. disease vs. control) with compare_groups().
  4. Visualize with plot_group_delta_heatmap(), plot_pair_boxplot(), or plot_volcano_groups().

Simulate a two-group dataset

How generate_sim() builds one sample

Before generating the full disease/control dataset, it helps to look at what a single sample produced by generate_sim() actually contains.

A sample is a flat data.frame of cells with x, y, and cell_type columns. With test_type = "distribute":

  1. All cells are first dropped uniformly at random in a max_loc x max_loc box.
  2. Each cell is assigned one of n_types cell types.
  3. A fraction close_ratio of the cell_type_2 cells is then moved next to a randomly chosen cell_type_1 cell, at distance distance_param (with small Gaussian jitter).

So close_ratio controls the strength of the planted 1 ↔︎ 2 spatial interaction. distance_param controls how close the pairing is.

library(ggplot2)
#> Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.3.3

# A small parameter sweep on close_ratio, all other params fixed.
ratios  <- c(0.0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0)
df_list <- lapply(ratios, function(r) {
  d <- generate_sim(close_ratio    = r,
                    n_types        = 5,
                    n_cells        = 400,
                    max_loc        = 300,
                    test_type      = "distribute",
                    distance_param = 15,
                    seed           = 7)
  d$close_ratio <- sprintf("close_ratio = %.1f", r)
  d$.target     <- ifelse(as.character(d$cell_type) %in%
                            c("cell_type_1", "cell_type_2"),
                          as.character(d$cell_type), "other")
  d
})
df_sweep <- do.call(rbind, df_list)
df_sweep$close_ratio <- factor(df_sweep$close_ratio,
                               levels = sprintf("close_ratio = %.1f", ratios))

ggplot(df_sweep, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(data = subset(df_sweep, .target == "other"),
             color = "grey85", size = 0.35) +
  geom_point(data = subset(df_sweep, .target != "other"),
             aes(color = .target), size = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ close_ratio, nrow = 1) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(cell_type_1 = "#E41A1C", cell_type_2 = "#377EB8")) +
  labs(title = "Effect of close_ratio on one simulated sample",
       subtitle = "grey = other cell types, red = cell_type_1, blue = cell_type_2",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

As close_ratio grows from 0 to 1 you can see the red and blue points visibly clump into pairs while the grey background stays uniform. That clumping is exactly the signal nhood_enrichment should pick up.

To make distance_param concrete, zoom into one sample and draw a segment from each red seed to its paired blue partner:

one <- generate_sim(close_ratio    = 1.0,
                    n_types        = 5,
                    n_cells        = 300,
                    max_loc        = 300,
                    test_type      = "distribute",
                    distance_param = 25,
                    seed           = 42)

# Reconstruct the seed-partner pairs deterministically by re-running the
# seeding logic of generate_sim() so we can draw the connecting segments.
set.seed(42)
.x  <- runif(300, 0, 300); .y <- runif(300, 0, 300)
.ct <- sample(paste0("cell_type_", 1:5), 300, replace = TRUE)
i1  <- which(.ct == "cell_type_1")
i2  <- which(.ct == "cell_type_2")
n_pairs <- round(length(i2) * 1.0)
ic1 <- sample(i1, n_pairs, replace = TRUE)
ic2 <- sample(i2, n_pairs)

# Use the moved coordinates of cell_type_2 from the simulated sample,
# matched back by index.
segs <- data.frame(
  x = one$x[ic1], y = one$y[ic1],
  xend = one$x[ic2], yend = one$y[ic2]
)
# Keep only nearby pairs for clarity in the zoom
zoom <- segs[segs$x > 50 & segs$x < 230 & segs$y > 50 & segs$y < 230, ]

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = one, aes(x = x, y = y),
             color = "grey85", size = 0.4) +
  geom_segment(data = zoom,
               aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = subset(one, cell_type == "cell_type_1"),
             aes(x = x, y = y), color = "#E41A1C", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = subset(one, cell_type == "cell_type_2"),
             aes(x = x, y = y), color = "#377EB8", size = 1.2) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Each blue (cell_type_2) sits ≈ distance_param away from a red seed",
       subtitle = "lines connect each seed (cell_type_1) to its paired partner (cell_type_2)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())

generate_sim_groups() then calls generate_sim() once per sample, using a group-specific close_ratio (plus a small per-sample noise), so the result is n_samples_per_group x length(group_close_ratio) samples sharing the same coordinate space but differing in how strongly the 1 ↔︎ 2 interaction is planted.

set.seed(1)
df_groups <- generate_sim_groups(
  n_samples_per_group = 8,
  group_close_ratio = list(disease = 0.95, control = 0.05),
  n_types = 5,
  n_cells = 500,
  test_type = "distribute",
  distance_param = 10,
  between_sample_noise = 0.02,
  seed = 1
)
head(df_groups)

#> disease_1_cell1 239.64211 545.8865 cell_type_1 disease_1 disease disease_1
#> disease_1_cell2  78.11157 414.1219 cell_type_4 disease_1 disease disease_1
#> disease_1_cell3 239.06971 622.5321 cell_type_2 disease_1 disease disease_1

#> disease_1_cell5 300.35948 331.8670 cell_type_1 disease_1 disease disease_1
#> disease_1_cell6 584.28894 446.3800 cell_type_4 disease_1 disease disease_1
table(df_groups$sample_id, df_groups$group)
#>            
#>             control disease
#>   control_1     500       0
#>   control_2     500       0
#>   control_3     500       0

The settings above are tuned so the planted cell_type_1 ↔︎ cell_type_2 signal is strong enough that downstream compare_groups() reaches BH-adjusted significance across the full 5 × 5 cluster grid. With smaller n_samples_per_group or a narrower close_ratio gap, the Wilcoxon p-value floor combined with 25-pair multiple-testing correction often prevents padj < 0.05 even when the planted effect is real — keep that in mind when designing your own experiments.

df_groups is a long-format data.frame with columns x, y, cell_type, sample_id, group, patient. The same shape is what the *_per_sample() helpers accept directly; for Seurat input they read the equivalent fields from meta.data and @images.

Spatial map of the simulated samples

Before any statistics, it helps to see the planted structure: with test_type = "distribute" and group_close_ratio = list(disease = 0.85, control = 0.15), the disease samples should show clear local pairing of cell_type_1 (the seed type) and cell_type_2 (the partner placed at distance_param from each seed), while control samples should look nearly random.

library(ggplot2)

# Order panels so disease and control sit on contiguous rows
df_groups$sample_id <- factor(
  df_groups$sample_id,
  levels = unique(df_groups$sample_id[order(df_groups$group, df_groups$sample_id)])
)

ggplot(df_groups, aes(x = x, y = y, color = cell_type)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ group + sample_id, nrow = 4) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_manual(values = manual_colors[seq_len(nlevels(df_groups$cell_type))]) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2.5))) +
  labs(title = "Simulated samples by disease group",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, color = "cell type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
#> Warning: No shared levels found between `names(values)` of the manual scale and the

To highlight the planted interaction, restrict to the two seeded cell types and overlay them on a grey background of all other cells:

target <- c("cell_type_1", "cell_type_2")
df_groups$.target <- ifelse(as.character(df_groups$cell_type) %in% target,
                            as.character(df_groups$cell_type), "other")

ggplot(df_groups, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(data = subset(df_groups, .target == "other"),
             color = "grey85", size = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = subset(df_groups, .target != "other"),
             aes(color = .target), size = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ group + sample_id, nrow = 4) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(cell_type_1 = "#E41A1C", cell_type_2 = "#377EB8")) +
  labs(title = "Planted interaction: cell_type_1 vs cell_type_2",
       subtitle = "disease samples should show tight 1–2 pairing; control samples should not",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())


df_groups$.target <- NULL

Per-sample neighborhood enrichment

per_sample <- nhood_enrichment_per_sample(
  df_groups,
  sample_key   = "sample_id",
  group_key    = "group",
  cluster_key  = "cell_type",
  patient_key  = "patient",
  neighbors.k  = 12,
  n_perms      = 200,
  n_jobs       = 1,
  seed         = 1
)
head(per_sample)
#>   sample_id   cluster_i   cluster_j     zscore    count   group   patient
#> 1 control_1 cell_type_1 cell_type_1  4.0547626 26.59633 control control_1
#> 2 control_1 cell_type_2 cell_type_1 -0.5807198 16.84643 control control_1
#> 3 control_1 cell_type_3 cell_type_1 -0.8365583 18.54675 control control_1
#> 4 control_1 cell_type_4 cell_type_1 -1.1248416 17.31725 control control_1
#> 5 control_1 cell_type_5 cell_type_1 -0.7344125 19.41918 control control_1
#> 6 control_1 cell_type_1 cell_type_2 -2.2008546 16.47835 control control_1

Each row is sample_id x cluster_i x cluster_j. The factor levels of cell_type are harmonized across samples so that the cluster_i, cluster_j columns are directly comparable.

Sanity check: per-group enrichment heatmaps

Before running any statistical test it pays to plot the observed neighborhood enrichment z-score, averaged across samples within each group. If the simulator is working, the disease group should show a clearly positive z-score on the cell_type_1 ↔︎ cell_type_2 pair (planted by generate_sim() with close_ratio = 0.85), and the control group should be near zero everywhere.

library(ggplot2)

# Average the per-sample z-score within group (this is the input compare_groups
# will then test against zero between groups).
mean_z <- aggregate(zscore ~ cluster_i + cluster_j + group,
                    data = per_sample, FUN = function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))

# Symmetric color limits around 0 so disease vs control are directly comparable
lim <- max(abs(mean_z$zscore), na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(mean_z, aes(x = cluster_i, y = cluster_j, fill = zscore)) +
  geom_tile(color = "grey90", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", zscore)), size = 2.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ group) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-lim, lim)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Observed neighborhood enrichment z-score by group",
       subtitle = "mean across samples; planted signal is on cell_type_1 vs cell_type_2",
       x = "cluster i", y = "cluster j", fill = "mean z") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

The cell at (cell_type_1, cell_type_2) (and its symmetric counterpart) is the only one that should differ markedly between the two facets — and in particular it should be strongly positive in disease and near zero in control. Use this plot as a quick check that the simulation actually reflects the disease structure you intended before trusting the group-comparison p-values below.

You can also look at this group-mean object as a small table for a direct numeric comparison:

target_pair <- subset(mean_z,
                      cluster_i == "cell_type_1" & cluster_j == "cell_type_2")
target_pair
#>      cluster_i   cluster_j   group     zscore
#> 6  cell_type_1 cell_type_2 control -1.1695215
#> 31 cell_type_1 cell_type_2 disease  0.8866004

For the radius-based ratio, the local interaction score, and the interaction-spot count, use the parallel helpers:

cooccur_ratio_per_sample(
  df_groups, sample_key = "sample_id", group_key = "group",
  cluster_key = "cell_type", patient_key = "patient",
  radius = 30, k = 15
)

cooccur_local_per_sample(
  df_groups, sample_key = "sample_id", group_key = "group",
  cluster_key = "cell_type",
  cluster_x = "cell_type_1", cluster_y = "cell_type_2",
  patient_key = "patient",
  neighbors.k = 15, radius = 30
)

Group comparison

compare_groups() runs a per-cluster-pair test between two groups. Set ref_group to make the sign of effect interpretable (effect = mean(test) - mean(reference)).

Algorithm

Let \(S\) be the set of samples, \(G_s \in \{g_\mathrm{ref}, g_\mathrm{test}\}\) the group of sample \(s\), and \(V_{s,i,j}\) the per-sample score (e.g. the z-score from nhood_enrichment_per_sample()) for the ordered cluster pair \((i, j)\). compare_groups() iterates over every unique \((i, j)\) and runs the chosen two-group test on the vector \(\{V_{s,i,j}\}_{s \in S}\) split by \(G_s\).

For each pair it reports

\[ \hat{\mu}_g \;=\; \frac{1}{|S_g|}\sum_{s \in S_g} V_{s,i,j}, \qquad \widehat{\text{effect}}_{i,j} \;=\; \hat{\mu}_{g_\mathrm{test}} - \hat{\mu}_{g_\mathrm{ref}}, \]

where \(S_g = \{s : G_s = g\}\).

After all pairs are tested, raw \(p\)-values \(p_{i,j}\) are corrected for multiple testing across pairs:

\[ \tilde{p}_{i,j} \;=\; \mathrm{adjust}\bigl(\{p_{i,j}\};\, \text{method}\bigr), \]

defaulting to the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure (\(\tilde{p}_{(k)} = \min_{m \ge k}\bigl\{\frac{M}{m} p_{(m)}\bigr\}\), with \(M\) the number of pairs and \(p_{(k)}\) the \(k\)-th smallest \(p\)-value).

The four method choices differ only in how each per-pair \(p_{i,j}\) is computed.

method = "wilcox" — Wilcoxon rank-sum

Let \(V^{(\mathrm{ref})}\) and \(V^{(\mathrm{test})}\) denote the per-sample scores in each group (sizes \(n_1, n_2\)), and let \(R_k\) be the rank of \(V^{(\mathrm{test})}_k\) when all \(n_1 + n_2\) values are pooled and ranked. The Mann–Whitney \(U\) statistic is

\[ U \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{n_2} R_k \;-\; \frac{n_2(n_2+1)}{2}. \]

Under the null (\(V^{(\mathrm{ref})}\) and \(V^{(\mathrm{test})}\) share a distribution),

\[ \mathbb{E}[U] = \frac{n_1 n_2}{2}, \quad \mathrm{Var}(U) = \frac{n_1 n_2 (n_1 + n_2 + 1)}{12}, \]

and the two-sided \(p\)-value comes from the normal approximation in stats::wilcox.test(..., exact = FALSE).

This test is non-parametric and robust, which makes it the safest default when you have a handful of samples per group.

method = "t" — Welch’s two-sample \(t\)

Same per-pair split as above. Let \(\bar V_g\), \(s_g^2\) be the sample mean and unbiased variance in each group. Welch’s statistic is

\[ t \;=\; \frac{\bar V^{(\mathrm{test})} - \bar V^{(\mathrm{ref})}} {\sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}}} \]

with Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom

\[ \nu \;=\; \frac{\left(\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}\right)^2} {\dfrac{(s_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1 - 1} + \dfrac{(s_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2 - 1}}. \]

Use this if you trust approximate normality of the per-sample scores.

method = "lmm" — linear mixed model

When you have multiple images per patient, you should not treat them as independent observations. For a given pair \((i, j)\), write the score of image \(k\) from patient \(p\) as

\[ V_{p,k,i,j} \;=\; \beta_0 \;+\; \beta_1 \, \mathbb{1}\{G_{p,k} = g_\mathrm{test}\} \;+\; u_p \;+\; \varepsilon_{p,k}, \]

with random patient intercept \(u_p \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)\) and residuals \(\varepsilon_{p,k} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)\).

compare_groups() fits this with lme4::lmer(value ~ group + (1 | patient)), then tests \(H_0\!: \beta_1 = 0\) with a Wald-z approximation using the \(t\)-value from summary(fit)$coefficients:

\[ z \;=\; \frac{\hat\beta_1}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat\beta_1)}, \qquad p \;=\; 2\,\Phi(-|z|). \]

If each patient contributes only a single observation the LMM collapses to OLS and compare_groups() falls back to lm(). The Wald-z \(p\)-value is approximate; for stricter inference fit with lmerTest outside the package.

method = "perm" — group-label permutation

Let \(\Delta = \hat\mu_{g_\mathrm{test}} - \hat\mu_{g_\mathrm{ref}}\) be the observed mean difference for pair \((i, j)\). We then shuffle the group labels \(B\) times (n_perms) to build a null distribution.

Without patient_key, every permutation reassigns sample-level labels independently:

\[ \Delta^{(b)} \;=\; \hat\mu^{(b)}_{g_\mathrm{test}} - \hat\mu^{(b)}_{g_\mathrm{ref}}, \quad b = 1, \dots, B. \]

With patient_key, labels are shuffled at the patient level (each patient keeps the same label across all of its images), which preserves within-patient correlation.

The two-sided \(p\)-value uses the standard \(+1\)-smoothed estimator

\[ p \;=\; \frac{1 \;+\; \#\{b : |\Delta^{(b)}| \ge |\Delta|\}}{1 \;+\; B}, \]

avoiding \(p = 0\) in finite-\(B\) samples. This is the preferred method when the per-sample score distribution is far from normal or when you need patient-level blocking.

Multiple-testing adjustment

All \(p\)-values are passed through stats::p.adjust(..., method = adjust). The default "BH" controls the false discovery rate across the \(M\) tested cluster pairs at the chosen level \(\alpha\) by

\[ k^{*} \;=\; \max\Bigl\{k : p_{(k)} \le \frac{k}{M}\,\alpha\Bigr\}, \]

and rejecting all pairs with \(p_{(k)} \le p_{(k^*)}\). The returned padj column holds the BH-adjusted values directly, so a downstream \(\tilde p_{i,j} < \alpha\) check gives exactly the BH decision.

cmp_wilcox <- compare_groups(
  per_sample,
  value     = "zscore",
  method    = "wilcox",
  adjust    = "BH",
  ref_group = "control"
)
head(cmp_wilcox)

When you have multiple images per patient, prefer a mixed model (random intercept on patient) or a patient-blocked permutation:

cmp_lmm <- compare_groups(
  per_sample,
  value       = "zscore",
  method      = "lmm",
  patient_key = "patient",
  ref_group   = "control"
)

Visualization

plot_group_delta_heatmap(cmp_wilcox)
plot_volcano_groups(cmp_wilcox, label_top = 5)
plot_pair_boxplot(
  per_sample,
  value     = "zscore",
  pairs     = data.frame(cluster_i = "cell_type_1",
                         cluster_j = "cell_type_2"),
  add_p     = TRUE,
  ref_group = "control"
)

Patient-level aggregation

If you have multiple images per patient and want one observation per patient, pass unit = "patient" to the *_per_sample() helpers. Each image-level result is then averaged within patient before group comparison:

per_patient <- nhood_enrichment_per_sample(
  df_groups, sample_key = "sample_id", group_key = "group",
  cluster_key = "cell_type", patient_key = "patient",
  unit = "patient",
  neighbors.k = 15, n_perms = 100, n_jobs = 1
)

Inputs other than a data.frame

All *_per_sample() helpers accept three kinds of input:

  • A Seurat object with multiple images. sample_key is a column of meta.data whose values match names(obj@images).
  • A list of Seurat objects, where each may itself have multiple images. source_index in build_sample_design() records the list origin.
  • A data.frame with x, y, the cluster column, and the sample / group / (optional) patient columns.

build_sample_design() is the small helper that turns any of these into the design table used downstream — call it directly if you only want the sample / group / patient mapping.

build_sample_design(
  df_groups,
  sample_key  = "sample_id",
  group_key   = "group",
  patient_key = "patient"
)
#>           sample_id   group   patient source_index
